content: A nosebleed refers to the loss of blood from the tissue lining the inside of the nose. Typically, the bleeding occurs in one nostril. Nosebleeds are a common occurrence and are often caused by minor irritations or colds. While they can be alarming for some individuals, they are rarely life-threatening. The nose contains numerous small blood vessels that are prone to bleeding. Air passing through the nose can dry out and irritate the membranes lining the nasal passages, leading to the formation of crusts. These crusts may bleed when disturbed by actions such as rubbing, picking, or blowing the nose. The nasal lining is more likely to become dry and irritated in conditions of low humidity, allergies, colds, or sinus infections. Consequently, nosebleeds are more frequent during the winter months when viral infections are prevalent, and indoor heating dries out the air. Other causes of nosebleeds include a deviated nasal septum, the presence of a foreign object in the nose, or other forms of nasal obstruction. Most nosebleeds originate from the front part of the nasal septum, which is the tissue dividing the two sides of the nose. This area contains fragile blood vessels that are easily damaged. These anterior nosebleeds are generally straightforward for a trained professional to manage. Less commonly, nosebleeds may occur higher up on the septum or deeper within the nasal cavity, which can be more challenging to control. Causes of Nosebleeds Nosebleeds can result from various factors, including: Allergic rhinitis A foreign object lodged in the nose Barotrauma (pressure-related injury) Forceful nose blowing Exposure to chemical irritants Direct trauma to the nose, such as a broken nose Nose picking Overuse of decongestant nasal sprays Repeated sneezing Facial or nasal surgery Use of high doses of aspirin or blood-thinning medications Upper respiratory infections Extremely cold or dry air Recurrent nosebleeds may indicate an underlying condition, such as high blood pressure, allergies, a bleeding disorder, or a tumor in the nasal or sinus region. High-Risk Groups Occasionally, frequent nosebleeds may signal other medical conditions, such as bleeding disorders or hypertension. Repeated nosebleeds can also be a symptom of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome. Blood-thinning medications, such as Coumadin, Plavix, or aspirin, can cause or exacerbate nosebleeds. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Emergency medical attention is necessary if: Bleeding persists for more than 20 minutes. A nosebleed occurs following a head injury, as this may indicate a skull fracture and require imaging studies. The nose appears deformed after trauma, suggesting a possible nasal fracture. You should contact your doctor if you or your child experiences frequent nosebleeds, especially if they are becoming more common and are not associated with minor irritations like colds. Treatment Options To manage a nosebleed: 1. Sit down and gently pinch the soft part of the nose between your thumb and index finger, keeping the nostrils closed for a full 10 minutes. 2. Lean forward to prevent swallowing blood and breathe through your mouth. 3. Wait at least 10 minutes before checking if the bleeding has stopped. Allowing sufficient time is crucial for the bleeding to cease. 4. Applying a cold compress or ice across the bridge of the nose may help. 5. Avoid packing the nose with gauze. 6. Do not lie down during a nosebleed. 7. Refrain from sniffing or blowing your nose for several hours after the bleeding stops. If bleeding continues, a nasal spray decongestant (e.g., Afrin or Neo-Synephrine) may help constrict small blood vessels and control the bleeding. Medical Care for Nosebleeds If necessary, seek medical attention at a hospital or clinic specializing in treating nosebleeds. What to Expect (Prognosis) A physician will perform a physical examination and may monitor for signs of hypovolemic shock in severe cases. The doctor will ask detailed questions about the nosebleeds, such as: Is the bleeding heavy? Does the bleeding stop quickly with pressure on the nostrils? When did the nosebleeds begin? Are they frequent or recurrent? Does the bleeding occur on one or both sides of the nose? Are there any accompanying symptoms? Is there blood in the stool or vomit? Do you bruise or bleed easily? Are there small red or purple spots on the skin (petechiae)? Are you taking blood-thinning medications like Coumadin or aspirin? Diagnostic tests may include: Complete blood count (CBC) Nasal endoscopy (using a camera to examine the nasal passages) Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) measurements Prothrombin time (PT) CT scan of the nose and sinuses Treatment will focus on addressing the underlying cause of the nosebleeds and may involve: Controlling blood pressure Cauterizing the blood vessel using heat, electric current, or silver nitrate sticks Nasal packing Reducing a broken nose or removing a foreign object Adjusting or discontinuing blood-thinning medications or aspirin Referral to an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist may be necessary for further diagnosis and treatment. Prevention of Nosebleeds To prevent nosebleeds, consider the following measures: Use a vaporizer or humidifier to maintain humidity in the air, especially during winter. Apply nasal saline spray or water-soluble jelly (e.g., Ayr gel) to keep the nasal passages moist.
